items.title: Adjectives
items.html:
Adjective rules

  • An adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case, not always in declension or ending: agricola bonus, nauta fortis.
  • Most adjectives come after their noun; adjectives of size and quantity (magnus, multus, omnis) and demonstratives usually come before.
  • Used without a noun, an adjective stands for people or things: bonī (good men), multa (many things), omnia (everything).
  • Dictionary entries show the declension: bonus, -a, -um is 1st/2nd; omnis, -e or ingēns, -entis is 3rd.

1st/2nd declension adjectives: bonus, bona, bonum (good)

Masculine like servus, feminine like puella, neuter like bellum.

items.title: Conjugations
items.html:
The 5 conjugations: 6 tenses, active indicative

Find the conjugation from the infinitive: -āre 1st, -ēre 2nd, -ere 3rd (3rd -iō if the first part ends in -iō), -īre 4th. Present, imperfect and future are built on the present stem; perfect, pluperfect and future perfect are built on the perfect stem (3rd principal part minus -ī) and use the same endings in every conjugation.

items.title: Declensions
items.html:
The 5 declensions

The genitive singular shows the declension: -ae 1st, -ī 2nd, -is 3rd, -ūs 4th, -ēī/-eī 5th. Drop the genitive ending to get the stem.

Neuter rules (every declension)

  • Nominative, accusative and vocative are always the same.
  • Nominative and accusative plural always end in -a (-ia for 3rd declension i-stems, -ua for the 4th).
  • Every other case matches the masculine of that declension.

3rd declension i-stems

  • Genitive plural -ium; neuters also take ablative singular -ī and nominative plural -ia.
  • Parisyllabic nouns (same number of syllables in nominative and genitive: cīvis, cīvis), nouns with a one-syllable nominative ending in -s or -x after two consonants (urbs, urbis; nox, noctis), and neuters in -e, -al, -ar (mare, animal, exemplar).

items.title: Participles
items.html:
What a participle is

  • A verbal adjective: it comes from a verb, so it has tense and voice and can take objects or adverbs, but it declines like an adjective and agrees with a noun in gender, number and case.
  • Latin has three: present active (loving), perfect passive (having been loved) and future active (about to love).
  • Participle tense is relative to the main verb, not to now: present = at the same time, perfect = before, future = after.

Formation

ConjugationPresent activePerfect passiveFuture active
1st: amō, amāre, amāvī, amātusamāns, amantisamātus, -a, -umamātūrus, -a, -um
2nd: moneō, monēre, monuī, monitusmonēns, monentismonitus, -a, -ummonitūrus, -a, -um
3rd: regō, regere, rēxī, rēctusregēns, regentisrēctus, -a, -umrēctūrus, -a, -um
3rd -iō: capiō, capere, cēpī, captuscapiēns, capientiscaptus, -a, -umcaptūrus, -a, -um
4th: audiō, audīre, audīvī, audītusaudiēns, audientisaudītus, -a, -umaudītūrus, -a, -um
ParticipleHow to form itTranslation
Present activePresent stem + -ns (genitive -ntis): -āns in the 1st, -ēns in the 2nd and 3rd, -iēns in the 3rd -iō and 4thloving, while loving
Perfect passive4th principal part: drop nothing, it already ends in -us(having been) loved
Future activeStem of the 4th principal part + -ūrus, -ūra, -ūrumabout to love, going to love
  • sum has no present or perfect participle; its future participle is futūrus (about to be). eō: iēns, euntis. possum: potēns (powerful, used as an adjective).
  • Deponent verbs have a perfect participle with active meaning: cōnātus (having tried), secūtus (having followed), locūtus (having spoken), profectus (having set out), ēgressus (having gone out).

Declension

Present participle: 3rd declension, one ending (amāns, amantis)

CaseMasc./fem. sgNeut. sgMasc./fem. plNeut. pl
Nominativeamānsamānsamantēsamantia
Genitiveamantisamantisamantiumamantium
Dativeamantīamantīamantibusamantibus
Accusativeamantemamānsamantēsamantia
Ablativeamante (amantī)amante (amantī)amantibusamantibus
Vocativeamānsamānsamantēsamantia

Ablative singular -e when it acts as a verb (ā puerō clāmante), -ī when it is a plain adjective (ā virō sapientī). Genitive plural -ium, neuter plural -ia.

Perfect and future participles: like bonus, bona, bonum

portātus, portāta, portātum; portātūrus, portātūra, portātūrum. They take every 1st/2nd declension ending: portātī, portātae, portāta, portātōrum and so on.

Uses

UseWhat it doesExampleTranslation
AttributiveDescribes a noun like any adjectivepuerum dormientem vīdīI saw the sleeping boy
CircumstantialAdds when, why, although or if; translate with a clausemīlitēs urbem captam dēlēvēruntThe soldiers captured the city and destroyed it / destroyed the city after it had been captured
SubstantiveStands alone as a nounaudientēs plausērunt; captī clāmābantThe listeners applauded; the captives were shouting
Ablative absoluteNoun + participle in the ablative, not tied to the main clause grammaticallyurbe captā, Rōmānī discessēruntWhen the city had been captured, the Romans left
With sum (passive perfect system)Perfect participle + sum makes the perfect passiveepistula scrīpta estThe letter was written / has been written
Future active + sumActive periphrastic: intention or likelihooddiscessūrus sumI am about to leave, I intend to leave
Future active of purposeSometimes shows purpose after verbs of motionvēnit pugnātūrusHe came to fight

Relative time

ParticipleTime compared with the main verbExampleTranslation
PresentSame timesenem ambulantem salūtāvitHe greeted the old man (who was) walking
PerfectBeforesenem vulnerātum iūvitHe helped the old man who had been wounded
FutureAftersenem moritūrum cōnsōlātus estHe comforted the old man who was about to die

Ablative absolute

  • A noun or pronoun in the ablative plus a participle (or another noun or adjective, since sum has no present participle: Caesare duce, with Caesar as leader; mē invītō, against my will).
  • The noun cannot be the subject or object of the main verb; if it were, Latin would use an ordinary participle instead.
  • Translate with when, after, since, although or because, or with "with": hostibus vīsīs, when the enemy had been seen, after seeing the enemy.
  • Present: rēge regente, while the king was ruling. Perfect: signō datō, after the signal had been given.

Translation tips

  • Find the noun the participle agrees with first (same gender, number and case), then decide how it relates to the main verb.
  • Perfect passive participles are passive: servus captus is the slave who was captured, not who captured. For "having captured" Latin uses an ablative absolute or a cum clause, or a deponent.
  • A participle often sits far from its noun and can wrap around words that belong to it: ad urbem ā mīlitibus dēlētam, to the city destroyed by the soldiers.
  • Long participle phrases usually read best as a relative clause (who, which) or a when/after clause.
